newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Allianz, Munich Re to be unaccustomed rivals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Allianz, Munich Re to be unaccustomed rivals.

text.p: News of a mega-merger on the German insurance market has left Allianz AG facing an unaccustomed challenge from its Bavarian neighbour and traditional ally Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG.

Munich Re, co-founded with Allianz at the end of the 19th century, plans to merge its Hamburg-Mannheimer and DKV units with Victoria Holding AG to create the country's second-largest primary insurer after Allianz, with itself as majority owner.
"Very delicate," was the response on Friday from one senior insurance industry official to news of the merger, which emerged late on Thursday. He added that the move was an "interesting change".
Allianz and Munich Re have been closely connected for many years, with each company holding a 25 percent stake in the other.

But while for decades the companies had clearly separate interests -- Allianz pursuing global life and non-life business while Munich Re worked on becoming the world's leading reinsurer -- the boundaries between their business have become increasingly blurred.

And while once the two companies were linked through a complicated network of cross-shareholdings and jointly-managed units, they have been pushed further apart over the years due to pressure from the German cartel office.
The chasm can only widen as a result of the merger, which will raise Munich Re's premium income to some 46 billion marks ($26.3 billion), of which half will be related to primary insurance.
That will make it the second-largest player in German life and non-life insurance after Allianz which had global premium income of 74.6 billion marks in 1996.
Munich Re itself played down the development. Industry sources said the deal was almost certainly discussed in advance with Allianz.
Allianz itself owns 20 percent of Hamburg-Mannheimer, a holding it has said may change as a result of the merger.
"Nothing fundamental is changing in the relationship between Allianz and Munich Re," a spokesman said.
Allianz AG was more forthcoming.
"Naturally it is a challenge," a spokesman said. "We are expecting tougher competition on the German market."
Allianz's spokesman said the merger was a positive development for customers, who will benefit from tougher competition, and for the market, which will gain a solid new insurance stock.
Both companies said they had no plans to part with their cross-shareholding agreement.
Some analysts believe the time has come for Munich Re and Allianz to break apart, particularly if Munich Re ups its activities in primary insurance.
The merged group, to be called ERGO, will include for example D.A.S., Europe's leading legal protection insurer, and DKV, the Munich Re-controlled market leader in European private health insurance.
"I wouldn't be surprised to see Munich Re getting some cartel-related problems out of this," said one London-based analyst, who asked not to be named.
"After all, Allianz and Munich Re have basically sewn up the European market for health insurance between them. Somebody will have to ask questions, if not in Germany, then in Europe."
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.751 German Marks)
